units.title: Why sequence transduction needed a new architecture
units.objective: Explain why recurrent sequence transduction models limit parallel training in the paper's motivation.

lesson_steps.title: Start with the bottleneck
lesson_steps.content: The paper begins from sequence transduction tasks such as translation, where a model must transform one sequence into another. It argues that strong recurrent systems were accurate but hard to parallelize because positions are processed in order.

lesson_steps.title: Define the sequential constraint
lesson_steps.content: In recurrent models, each hidden state h_t depends on h_{t-1} and the input at position t. That dependency chain means computation inside one example cannot be fully parallel across positions, which becomes costly for long sequences.

lesson_steps.title: Trace the RNN path
lesson_steps.content: For a sentence of length n, a recurrent layer must advance through n sequential operations before all positions have been processed. Table 1 later summarizes this as O(n) sequential operations for recurrent layers, unlike O(1) for self-attention.

lesson_steps.title: Accuracy versus trainability
lesson_steps.content: The authors do not claim that recurrent models are ineffective; they describe them as established state of the art. The problem is architectural: recurrence forces a time-ordered computation pattern that blocks parallelism within each training example.

lesson_steps.title: Diagnose a bottleneck
lesson_steps.content: Use the paper's reasoning to classify whether a layer has the same bottleneck as an RNN. Focus on whether a position must wait for the previous position's hidden state before it can be computed.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: A model computes z_5 only after computing z_4, and z_4 only after z_3. What bottleneck from the paper does this illustrate?
lesson_steps.expected_response: It illustrates the sequential computation constraint: positions are aligned with computation steps, preventing full parallelization within an example.
lesson_steps.remediation: Draw the dependency chain z_3 -> z_4 -> z_5 and ask whether z_5 can be computed at the same time as z_3. If not, it has the same kind of sequential bottleneck described for recurrent models.

lesson_steps.title: Independent check
lesson_steps.content: Check whether the learner can connect the motivation to the formal comparison in the paper. A correct answer should mention both sequence-position dependence and reduced parallelization.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: In one or two sentences, explain why the authors wanted to reduce sequential computation in sequence transduction models.
lesson_steps.expected_response: They wanted to avoid the RNN-style dependency where each position's hidden state depends on the previous one. Reducing that sequential computation allows more parallel training, especially for longer sequences.
lesson_steps.remediation: Return to the phrase 'factor computation along the symbol positions' and contrast it with computing all positions in parallel. Then restate Table 1's O(n) sequential operations for recurrent layers.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: Sequence transduction is the paper's task setting, and recurrent models were the dominant baseline. The key motivation is not merely better scoring but escaping the sequential computation constraint so training can be more parallelizable.

mastery_criteria: Explains how recurrent hidden states create a position-by-position dependency chain.
Connects the dependency chain to limited within-example parallelization.
Uses Table 1's sequential-operation comparison to justify the motivation.
common_difficulties: Treating the paper as rejecting RNN accuracy rather than rejecting the computational bottleneck.
Confusing batching across examples with parallelization across positions inside one example.

units.title: The Transformer as an attention-only encoder-decoder
units.objective: Describe the Transformer as an encoder-decoder model that replaces recurrence and convolutions with attention-based layers.

lesson_steps.title: Name the proposed solution
lesson_steps.content: After identifying recurrence as a bottleneck, the paper proposes the Transformer. Its central claim is that sequence transduction can be done with attention mechanisms alone, dispensing with both recurrence and convolutions.

lesson_steps.title: Preserve the outer structure
lesson_steps.content: The Transformer still follows the familiar encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder maps input symbols to continuous representations, and the decoder generates output symbols from those representations one at a time.

lesson_steps.title: Read Figure 1 at a high level
lesson_steps.content: In Figure 1, the left stack is the encoder and the right stack is the decoder. The boxes inside are attention and feed-forward components, showing that the paper changes the internal layer design rather than abandoning encoder-decoder sequence transduction.

lesson_steps.title: Not just adding attention to an RNN
lesson_steps.content: Earlier high-performing systems often used attention together with a recurrent network. The Transformer is different because attention becomes the primary mechanism for drawing dependencies, not an add-on to recurrence.

lesson_steps.title: Classify an architecture statement
lesson_steps.content: Apply the overview claim by deciding whether a described model matches the paper's Transformer idea. Look for the combination of encoder-decoder structure and absence of recurrence or convolution as the main sequence layer.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: A model has an encoder and decoder, but the encoder is a stack of LSTMs with attention on top. Is that the Transformer described here? Why or why not?
lesson_steps.expected_response: No. It has an encoder-decoder structure and attention, but it still relies on recurrent LSTM layers, while the Transformer relies entirely on attention and feed-forward layers.
lesson_steps.remediation: Point to the abstract's phrase 'dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely' and ask which part of the hypothetical model violates that condition.

lesson_steps.title: State the architecture claim
lesson_steps.content: Assess whether the learner can state the paper's architectural novelty precisely. The answer should mention both what is retained and what is removed.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: What does the Transformer keep from earlier sequence transduction models, and what does it replace?
lesson_steps.expected_response: It keeps the encoder-decoder structure. It replaces recurrent and convolutional sequence layers with stacked self-attention, multi-head attention, and position-wise feed-forward layers.
lesson_steps.remediation: Separate the architecture into 'outer skeleton' and 'inner layers.' The outer skeleton remains encoder-decoder, while the inner recurrent/convolutional layers are replaced by attention-based components.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: The Transformer is attention-only in the sense that it removes recurrence and convolution from sequence representation learning. It still uses an encoder-decoder structure, so its novelty lies in the stacked attention and feed-forward layer design inside that structure.

mastery_criteria: Distinguishes the Transformer from attention-augmented RNN models.
Identifies the encoder and decoder as the preserved outer architecture.
Explains that recurrence and convolutions are removed from the main sequence modeling layers.
common_difficulties: Thinking 'attention-only' means there are no feed-forward layers or embeddings.
Thinking the Transformer discards the encoder-decoder idea entirely.

units.title: Attention as queries, keys, values, and weighted sums
units.objective: Explain the query-key-value formulation of attention and how it produces an output vector.

lesson_steps.title: Why define attention formally
lesson_steps.content: The Transformer depends on attention everywhere, so the paper first gives a general attention definition. This definition lets the same mechanism be reused for self-attention and encoder-decoder attention later.

lesson_steps.title: Queries, keys, and values
lesson_steps.content: An attention function maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output. The query is compared with each key, and the resulting compatibility scores determine how much of each value contributes to the output.

lesson_steps.title: Follow one output computation
lesson_steps.content: For one query, imagine three key-value pairs. If the query is most compatible with the second key, the softmax weight on the second value will be largest, so the output weighted sum will be dominated by that value.

lesson_steps.title: Why this supports sequence modeling
lesson_steps.content: In a sequence, each position can supply a query while all positions supply keys and values. That is how attention can relate one position to other positions without stepping through them recurrently.

lesson_steps.title: Identify the roles
lesson_steps.content: Guide the learner to use the terminology precisely. The important distinction is that keys are used for matching, while values are the information that gets averaged into the output.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: In the paper's attention definition, which vectors are compared to decide weights, and which vectors are combined to make the output?
lesson_steps.expected_response: Queries are compared with keys to decide the weights. Values are combined as a weighted sum to produce the output.
lesson_steps.remediation: Use the phrase 'compatibility function of the query with the corresponding key' from the paper, then point out that the output is a weighted sum of values, not keys.

lesson_steps.title: Apply the mechanism independently
lesson_steps.content: Assess whether the learner can reason from scores to an output. They should not need exact numeric softmax values, only the relationship between compatibility and value contribution.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: If a query has much higher compatibility with key A than key B, what happens to the corresponding values in the attention output?
lesson_steps.expected_response: The value paired with key A receives a larger softmax weight and contributes more to the weighted-sum output than the value paired with key B.
lesson_steps.remediation: Restate attention as two stages: score query-key pairs, then use the resulting weights to average values. Emphasize that the key selects, while the value supplies content.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: Attention uses queries to choose among key-value pairs. Softmax converts compatibility scores into weights, and the output is a weighted sum of the values.

mastery_criteria: Correctly assigns matching to query-key comparisons.
Correctly assigns output content to weighted values.
Explains why attention can connect positions without recurrent stepping.
common_difficulties: Saying keys rather than values are averaged into the output.
Treating attention weights as learned constants rather than query-dependent softmax results.

units.title: Scaled dot-product attention formula
units.objective: Compute and interpret the scaled dot-product attention expression softmax(QK^T / sqrt(dk))V.

lesson_steps.title: Why the exact formula matters
lesson_steps.content: The paper's attention layer must be efficient enough to replace recurrent and convolutional layers. Scaled dot-product attention gives a matrix-multiplication-friendly formula for computing many attention outputs at once.

lesson_steps.title: State the formula
lesson_steps.content: The inputs are matrices Q, K, and V holding many queries, keys, and values. The Transformer computes Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(dk))V, where dk is the key and query dimension.

lesson_steps.title: Trace the matrix flow
lesson_steps.content: First QK^T forms all query-key dot products, so each row corresponds to one query's scores over all keys. Then the scores are scaled, softmaxed into weights, and multiplied by V to produce weighted sums of value vectors.

lesson_steps.title: Why scale the dot products
lesson_steps.content: Dot-product attention without scaling can produce large-magnitude scores when dk is large. The authors argue that large scores push softmax into regions with extremely small gradients, so dividing by sqrt(dk) counteracts that effect.

lesson_steps.title: Order the operations
lesson_steps.content: Have the learner reconstruct the computation in sequence. This checks whether they understand that scaling and softmax happen before values are combined.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: Put these steps in order: multiply by V, compute QK^T, apply softmax, divide by sqrt(dk).
lesson_steps.expected_response: Compute QK^T, divide by sqrt(dk), apply softmax, then multiply by V.
lesson_steps.remediation: Point to the formula and read it from the inside outward: QK^T is inside the softmax after scaling, and the final result multiplies V.

lesson_steps.title: Explain the scaling term
lesson_steps.content: Assess whether the learner can justify the scaling rather than merely name it. A full answer should mention large dot products, softmax saturation, and gradients.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: Why does the Transformer divide dot products by sqrt(dk) in scaled dot-product attention?
lesson_steps.expected_response: For large dk, dot products can grow large in magnitude, which can push softmax into regions with very small gradients. Dividing by sqrt(dk) reduces that problem.
lesson_steps.remediation: Use the paper's footnote intuition: summing dk independent products gives variance dk. Larger variance means larger score magnitudes, so scaling normalizes the scores before softmax.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: Scaled dot-product attention is a compact matrix formula for query-key matching and value averaging. The sqrt(dk) divisor is not cosmetic; it stabilizes softmax behavior when key/query dimensions are large.

mastery_criteria: Orders the operations in the scaled dot-product attention formula.
Explains the role of QK^T, softmax, and multiplication by V.
Justifies the sqrt(dk) scaling using the paper's gradient-saturation argument.
common_difficulties: Multiplying by V before softmaxing the compatibility scores.
Explaining scaling as a parameter learned by the model rather than a fixed normalization.

units.title: Multi-head attention and representation subspaces
units.objective: Explain how multi-head attention uses learned projections and parallel heads to attend to different information.

lesson_steps.title: Why one attention pass may be limiting
lesson_steps.content: A single attention head averages information according to one set of weights. The paper argues that this can inhibit attending to different types of information at different positions, so it introduces multiple heads.

lesson_steps.title: Define multi-head attention
lesson_steps.content: Multi-head attention linearly projects Q, K, and V h times into smaller subspaces. Each projected triplet runs scaled dot-product attention in parallel, the head outputs are concatenated, and a final projection produces the result.

lesson_steps.title: Read the figure and equation together
lesson_steps.content: Figure 2 shows several scaled dot-product attention modules running side by side before concatenation. In the base model, h = 8 and dk = dv = dmodel / h = 64, so total cost stays similar to one full-dimensional head.

lesson_steps.title: Why projections matter
lesson_steps.content: The learned projections are what let different heads operate in different representation subspaces. Without them, multiple heads would not have the same opportunity to specialize in distinct relations.

lesson_steps.title: Predict the head dimensions
lesson_steps.content: Use the base-model numbers to apply the relation between dmodel and per-head dimension. This reinforces the paper's point that heads split the representation rather than multiplying the full cost by h.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: In the base model, dmodel = 512 and h = 8. What are dk and dv for each head according to the paper?
lesson_steps.expected_response: dk = dv = dmodel / h = 512 / 8 = 64.
lesson_steps.remediation: Show that each head receives a fraction of the model dimension. The paper chooses smaller per-head dimensions so the combined cost is similar to single-head full-dimensional attention.

lesson_steps.title: Interpret the ablation
lesson_steps.content: Assess whether the learner can connect the mechanism to Table 3. The strongest answer notes that one head performs worse and too many heads can also reduce quality.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: Table 3 varies the number of attention heads while keeping computation roughly constant. What does this suggest about using multiple heads?
lesson_steps.expected_response: Multiple heads help because the single-head version is worse, but simply adding many heads is not always better; quality drops with too many heads in the reported settings.
lesson_steps.remediation: Compare the row with h = 1 to the base h = 8 row, then compare h = 32. Ask what pattern is supported rather than assuming monotonic improvement.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: Multi-head attention runs several smaller attention functions in parallel over learned projections. Its purpose is to let the model jointly attend to different positions and representation subspaces without greatly increasing computational cost.

mastery_criteria: Traces the projection, parallel attention, concatenation, and output projection steps.
Computes per-head dimensions from dmodel and h for the base model.
Interprets the head-count ablation without assuming more heads always help.
common_difficulties: Thinking each head uses the full dmodel dimension in the base cost comparison.
Treating heads as independent models rather than parallel sublayers whose outputs are recombined.

units.title: Encoder stack layer mechanics
units.objective: Describe the two sublayers and residual-normalization pattern in each Transformer encoder layer.

lesson_steps.title: Move from attention to a full layer
lesson_steps.content: Attention alone is not the whole encoder layer. The paper stacks self-attention with a position-wise feed-forward network and wraps each sublayer with residual addition and layer normalization.

lesson_steps.title: Two sublayers per encoder layer
lesson_steps.content: Each encoder layer has a multi-head self-attention sublayer followed by a position-wise fully connected feed-forward sublayer. The model uses N = 6 identical encoder layers in the reported architecture.

lesson_steps.title: Trace one encoder position
lesson_steps.content: At a given encoder layer, a token representation first attends to all positions in the previous encoder layer through multi-head self-attention. The result is added to the original sublayer input, normalized, passed through the feed-forward network, added again through a residual connection, and normalized again.

lesson_steps.title: Feed-forward formula
lesson_steps.content: The position-wise feed-forward network is FFN(x) = max(0, xW1 + b1)W2 + b2. It is applied separately and identically at each position, with input and output dimension dmodel = 512 and inner dimension dff = 2048 in the base model.

lesson_steps.title: Identify a missing sublayer
lesson_steps.content: Ask the learner to check an encoder-layer description against the paper's definition. The key is that each encoder layer contains both attention and feed-forward processing, each with Add & Norm.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: A proposed encoder layer has only multi-head self-attention followed by layer normalization. What component from the paper's encoder layer is missing?
lesson_steps.expected_response: It is missing the position-wise feed-forward network, and the full layer should also use residual addition followed by layer normalization around each sublayer.
lesson_steps.remediation: Point to Figure 1's encoder block: Multi-Head Attention, Add & Norm, Feed Forward, Add & Norm. Have the learner count the two sublayers and two Add & Norm operations.

lesson_steps.title: State the layer computation
lesson_steps.content: Assess whether the learner can explain the encoder layer as a sequence of operations. The answer should include self-attention, feed-forward network, residual connection, and layer normalization.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: Describe one Transformer encoder layer in the paper, including how residual connections and layer normalization are used.
lesson_steps.expected_response: One encoder layer applies multi-head self-attention, then adds the sublayer input and layer-normalizes. It then applies a position-wise feed-forward network, again adds the sublayer input and layer-normalizes.
lesson_steps.remediation: Use the formula LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)) and ask the learner to apply it twice: once to self-attention and once to the feed-forward network.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: The encoder is a stack of six identical layers in the base architecture. Each layer combines global self-attention with local position-wise transformation, stabilized by residual connections and layer normalization.

mastery_criteria: Lists the encoder layer's two sublayers in order.
Uses LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)) to explain Add & Norm.
Explains that the feed-forward network is applied separately but identically at each position.
common_difficulties: Forgetting the feed-forward sublayer because attention is the paper's headline idea.
Confusing identical application across positions with shared parameters across different layers.

units.title: Decoder stack, masking, and encoder-decoder attention
units.objective: Explain how the decoder preserves auto-regressive generation while attending to encoder outputs.

lesson_steps.title: Why the decoder needs extra rules
lesson_steps.content: The decoder must generate a target sequence one symbol at a time. Because of that, it must use attention without allowing a position to look at future target tokens during training.

lesson_steps.title: Three sublayers in the decoder
lesson_steps.content: Each decoder layer includes masked multi-head self-attention, multi-head attention over encoder outputs, and a position-wise feed-forward network. Like the encoder, each sublayer is wrapped with residual connections followed by layer normalization.

lesson_steps.title: Trace prediction at position i
lesson_steps.content: For output position i, masked self-attention can attend only to decoder positions up to and including i. Then encoder-decoder attention uses the decoder representation as a query and the encoder outputs as keys and values, allowing the prediction to use the full input sequence.

lesson_steps.title: Masking is not input masking
lesson_steps.content: The mask discussed here is not about hiding source-sentence tokens from the encoder. It prevents leftward information flow in the decoder's softmax by setting illegal future-position scores to negative infinity.

lesson_steps.title: Decide what a position may attend to
lesson_steps.content: Use a concrete target position to apply the masking rule. The learner should distinguish decoder self-attention from encoder-decoder attention.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: When predicting target position 4, which target positions may decoder self-attention use, and can encoder-decoder attention use all source positions?
lesson_steps.expected_response: Decoder self-attention may use target positions 1 through 4, not later target positions. Encoder-decoder attention can attend over all encoder output positions from the source sequence.
lesson_steps.remediation: Separate the two attention layers: masked self-attention controls target-side history, while encoder-decoder attention reads the already encoded source sequence.

lesson_steps.title: Explain the auto-regressive guarantee
lesson_steps.content: Assess whether the learner can connect masking and shifted outputs to auto-regressive decoding. The answer should identify future-token leakage as the problem being prevented.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: Why does the Transformer decoder mask subsequent positions in self-attention?
lesson_steps.expected_response: It masks subsequent positions so the prediction for position i can depend only on known outputs before or at i, preserving auto-regressive generation and preventing access to future target tokens.
lesson_steps.remediation: Ask what would happen if position i could attend to the correct token at position i+1 during training. Then explain that the mask makes those future connections illegal before the softmax.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: The decoder has one more attention sublayer than the encoder because it must read encoder outputs. Masked self-attention protects the auto-regressive property, while encoder-decoder attention connects each target position to the source representation.

mastery_criteria: Lists the decoder's three sublayers in order.
Explains how masking prevents future target-token access.
Distinguishes decoder self-attention from encoder-decoder attention in terms of Q, K, and V sources.
common_difficulties: Thinking the decoder mask blocks source tokens rather than future target positions.
Forgetting that encoder-decoder attention uses encoder outputs as keys and values.

units.title: Embeddings, output probabilities, and positional information
units.objective: Explain why the Transformer adds positional encodings to embeddings and how outputs become token probabilities.

lesson_steps.title: Why order must be injected
lesson_steps.content: The Transformer removes recurrence and convolution, so token order is not automatically built into the computation. The paper therefore adds positional encodings to token embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks.

lesson_steps.title: Embedding and output layers
lesson_steps.content: Input and output tokens are converted to learned vectors of dimension dmodel. The decoder's final vectors are converted to next-token probabilities by a learned linear transformation followed by softmax.

lesson_steps.title: Show the positional formulas
lesson_steps.content: The sinusoidal encoding uses PE(pos,2i) = sin(pos / 10000^{2i/dmodel}) and PE(pos,2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^{2i/dmodel}). These vectors have the same dimension as embeddings, so the model can add them directly to token embeddings.

lesson_steps.title: Sinusoidal versus learned positions
lesson_steps.content: The authors also tested learned positional embeddings and found nearly identical results. They chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow extrapolation to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training.

lesson_steps.title: Explain why dimensions match
lesson_steps.content: Guide the learner to reason from addition. If two vectors are added elementwise, the positional encoding and token embedding must share dmodel.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: Why do positional encodings in the paper have the same dimension dmodel as token embeddings?
lesson_steps.expected_response: They must have the same dimension so the positional encoding vector can be added elementwise to the token embedding vector.
lesson_steps.remediation: Write 'embedding + positional encoding' and ask what vector-shape condition is needed for addition. Then point to the paper's statement that both have dimension dmodel.

lesson_steps.title: Explain the need for positions
lesson_steps.content: Assess whether the learner can connect positional encoding to the absence of recurrence and convolution. A correct answer should mention order information, not just extra parameters.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: Why are positional encodings necessary in the Transformer architecture described in the paper?
lesson_steps.expected_response: Because the model has no recurrence or convolution, it needs another way to provide information about token order. Positional encodings inject absolute or relative position information by being added to embeddings.
lesson_steps.remediation: Contrast with an RNN, where processing order is tied to time steps. In the Transformer, all positions can be processed in parallel, so order must be represented explicitly in the input vectors.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: Embeddings turn tokens into dmodel-dimensional vectors, and output softmax turns decoder states into next-token probabilities. Positional encodings are added to embeddings so an attention-only model can represent sequence order.

mastery_criteria: Explains why positional encodings are needed without recurrence or convolution.
Interprets the sine/cosine formulas as fixed position vectors added to embeddings.
Distinguishes sinusoidal encodings from learned positional embeddings using the paper's stated rationale.
common_difficulties: Thinking positional encodings replace token embeddings rather than being added to them.
Assuming learned positional embeddings performed much worse, when Table 3 shows nearly identical results.

units.title: Why self-attention improves paths and parallelism
units.objective: Use Table 1 to compare self-attention with recurrent and convolutional layers on complexity, sequential operations, and maximum path length.

lesson_steps.title: Turn the design into criteria
lesson_steps.content: The paper does not justify self-attention only by intuition. It compares layer types using computational complexity, parallelizability, and maximum path length between positions.

lesson_steps.title: Define the three criteria
lesson_steps.content: Computational complexity measures total work per layer, while sequential operations measure how much of that work must be done in order. Maximum path length measures how many steps signals traverse between distant positions, which affects learning long-range dependencies.

lesson_steps.title: Read Table 1
lesson_steps.content: Table 1 gives self-attention O(n^2 d) complexity, O(1) sequential operations, and O(1) maximum path length. Recurrent layers have O(n d^2) complexity, O(n) sequential operations, and O(n) maximum path length.

lesson_steps.title: Where self-attention is not automatically cheapest
lesson_steps.content: Self-attention's O(n^2 d) term means it can be expensive for very long sequences. The paper notes it is faster than recurrent layers when sequence length n is smaller than representation dimension d, which is common in the translation settings discussed.

lesson_steps.title: Restricted attention as a tradeoff
lesson_steps.content: For very long sequences, the authors suggest restricted self-attention over a neighborhood of size r. That reduces complexity to O(r n d) but increases maximum path length to O(n/r), showing a tradeoff between efficiency and direct long-range connection.

lesson_steps.title: Compare two layer types
lesson_steps.content: Ask the learner to use the table rather than memory. The target reasoning is that the best path length and sequential-operation values explain the paper's preference for self-attention.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: According to Table 1, which layer type has O(1) sequential operations and O(1) maximum path length, and why is that useful?
lesson_steps.expected_response: Self-attention has O(1) sequential operations and O(1) maximum path length. This supports parallel computation and makes long-range dependencies easier to learn because positions are directly connected.
lesson_steps.remediation: Point to the row for Self-Attention and read across the two columns. Then connect O(1) operations to parallelization and O(1) path length to shorter signal paths.

lesson_steps.title: Reason about long sequences
lesson_steps.content: Assess whether the learner can identify the tradeoff rather than giving a blanket answer. The answer should mention that restricted attention lowers complexity but lengthens paths.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: Why might the paper consider restricted self-attention for very long sequences, and what cost does it introduce?
lesson_steps.expected_response: It may reduce computational cost by attending only to a neighborhood, changing complexity to O(r n d). The cost is a larger maximum path length, O(n/r), so distant positions are less directly connected.
lesson_steps.remediation: Frame full attention as 'everyone can see everyone' and restricted attention as 'only nearby positions are visible.' Less visibility reduces work but requires more steps for distant information to travel.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: Self-attention is attractive because it maximizes parallelism and minimizes path length between positions. Its quadratic dependence on sequence length motivates restricted variants for very long inputs, but those variants trade away some direct long-range access.

mastery_criteria: Uses Table 1 to compare self-attention, recurrent, and convolutional layers.
Explains why maximum path length matters for long-range dependencies.
Describes the efficiency-path-length tradeoff of restricted self-attention.
common_difficulties: Claiming self-attention is always computationally cheaper regardless of sequence length.
Confusing total computational complexity with minimum sequential operations.

units.title: Training data, batching, and optimizer schedule
units.objective: Summarize the training data, batching strategy, hardware schedule, and Adam learning-rate formula used for Transformer training.

lesson_steps.title: Why training details matter
lesson_steps.content: The paper's claims include both quality and training efficiency, so the training setup is part of the evidence. Data size, batching, hardware, and optimizer schedule all shape the reported results.

lesson_steps.title: Datasets and tokenization
lesson_steps.content: For English-German, the paper uses WMT 2014 with about 4.5 million sentence pairs and byte-pair encoding with a shared vocabulary of about 37,000 tokens. For English-French, it uses 36 million sentence pairs and a 32,000 word-piece vocabulary.

lesson_steps.title: Batching by token count
lesson_steps.content: Sentence pairs are batched by approximate sequence length. Each batch contains roughly 25,000 source tokens and 25,000 target tokens, which keeps batches comparable by token workload rather than sentence count alone.

lesson_steps.title: Optimizer and warmup
lesson_steps.content: Training uses Adam with beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.98, and epsilon = 10^-9. The learning rate increases linearly for 4,000 warmup steps and then decreases proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number, scaled by dmodel^-0.5.

lesson_steps.title: Read the schedule qualitatively
lesson_steps.content: The learner does not need to compute exact learning rates, but should interpret the two phases. The warmup phase raises the rate, and the later phase decays it.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: According to the learning-rate formula, what happens before and after warmup_steps = 4000?
lesson_steps.expected_response: Before 4000 steps, the learning rate increases linearly. Afterward, it decreases roughly with the inverse square root of the step number.
lesson_steps.remediation: Point to the min() expression: one term decreases as step_num^-0.5, while the warmup term grows with step_num until the crossover. Then summarize the shape as warm up, then decay.

lesson_steps.title: Summarize the regime
lesson_steps.content: Assess whether the learner can give a grounded summary without inventing details. A correct answer should include WMT data, subword tokenization, token-based batching, Adam, and warmup-decay scheduling.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: Give a concise summary of the paper's training regime for the translation models.
lesson_steps.expected_response: The models are trained on WMT 2014 translation datasets encoded with byte-pair or word-piece subword vocabularies, batched by approximate length with about 25,000 source and target tokens per batch. Training uses Adam with the specified beta values and a learning rate that warms up for 4000 steps and then decays by inverse square root.
lesson_steps.remediation: Organize the answer into four headings: data, tokenization, batching, and optimizer schedule. Revisit Section 5.1 and 5.3 under those headings.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: The reported Transformer results depend on large WMT datasets, subword vocabularies, length-aware token batching, and a specialized Adam schedule. The learning rate schedule has two phases: linear warmup followed by inverse-square-root decay.

mastery_criteria: Identifies the WMT datasets and subword tokenization choices used in training.
Explains batching by approximate sequence length and token count.
Interprets the learning-rate schedule as warmup followed by inverse-square-root decay.
common_difficulties: Confusing word-piece and byte-pair encodings across the two translation datasets.
Treating the learning rate as constant throughout training.

units.title: Regularization and inference choices
units.objective: Explain how dropout, label smoothing, checkpoint averaging, and beam search affect reported Transformer evaluation.

lesson_steps.title: Why evaluation is more than architecture
lesson_steps.content: The architecture is central, but reported BLEU also depends on training and inference choices. The paper specifies regularization and decoding methods so the results can be interpreted accurately.

lesson_steps.title: Residual dropout
lesson_steps.content: The paper applies dropout to each sublayer output before it is added to the sublayer input and normalized. It also applies dropout to the sum of embeddings and positional encodings in both encoder and decoder stacks.

lesson_steps.title: Label smoothing
lesson_steps.content: Label smoothing with value 0.1 makes the model less certain about target labels during training. The paper notes that this hurts perplexity but improves accuracy and BLEU score.

lesson_steps.title: Decode and average checkpoints
lesson_steps.content: For translation, base models average the last five checkpoints and big models average the last twenty. The paper then uses beam search with beam size 4 and length penalty alpha = 0.6, terminating early when possible.

lesson_steps.title: Interpret a metric tradeoff
lesson_steps.content: Use label smoothing to practice separating perplexity from BLEU. The learner should recognize that worse perplexity does not necessarily mean worse translation quality in these results.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: The paper says label smoothing hurts perplexity but improves BLEU. How should you interpret that?
lesson_steps.expected_response: Label smoothing makes the model less overconfident, which can increase perplexity, but it improves prediction quality as measured by accuracy and BLEU in the experiments.
lesson_steps.remediation: Explain that perplexity rewards assigning high probability to the exact target labels, while label smoothing deliberately softens those targets. The paper reports the practical outcome: better accuracy and BLEU despite worse perplexity.

lesson_steps.title: Use the ablation evidence
lesson_steps.content: Assess whether the learner can connect dropout to overfitting using Table 3. A correct answer should note that dropout is helpful and that the table varies dropout settings.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: What does Table 3 suggest about dropout in the Transformer experiments?
lesson_steps.expected_response: It suggests dropout is very helpful in avoiding overfitting, since rows varying Pdrop show worse or different development performance when dropout is removed or changed.
lesson_steps.remediation: Point to the row group where Pdrop is varied and compare development BLEU and perplexity. Then connect this to the authors' statement that dropout is very helpful in avoiding over-fitting.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: Regularization in the paper includes residual dropout and label smoothing, each affecting training behavior and evaluation metrics. Reported translation outputs also depend on checkpoint averaging and beam search, so those choices are part of the experimental recipe.

mastery_criteria: Explains where residual dropout is applied in the Transformer.
Explains why label smoothing can lower perplexity performance while improving BLEU.
Describes the paper's beam search and checkpoint averaging choices for translation evaluation.
common_difficulties: Assuming perplexity and BLEU must always improve together.
Ignoring decoding choices when interpreting reported BLEU scores.

units.title: Machine translation results and training cost
units.objective: Interpret Table 2's BLEU and training-cost comparisons for base and big Transformers.

lesson_steps.title: Connect architecture to evidence
lesson_steps.content: The paper's main empirical claim is that the Transformer improves translation quality while costing less to train. Table 2 is the central evidence for that claim on WMT 2014 English-German and English-French.

lesson_steps.title: Metrics in the table
lesson_steps.content: BLEU measures translation quality, while training cost is estimated in floating-point operations. The table compares single models, ensembles, base Transformer, and big Transformer across English-German and English-French.

lesson_steps.title: Read the English-German result
lesson_steps.content: On English-German, Transformer big reaches 28.4 BLEU. The paper states that this beats the best previously reported models, including ensembles, by more than 2 BLEU.

lesson_steps.title: Read the cost claim
lesson_steps.content: The base Transformer reaches 27.3 BLEU on English-German with an estimated training cost of 3.3 * 10^18 FLOPs. The big Transformer costs more, 2.3 * 10^19 FLOPs, but still compares favorably with many prior high-performing systems listed in the table.

lesson_steps.title: Make a supported comparison
lesson_steps.content: Practice interpreting both axes of the table. The learner should not focus only on BLEU or only on cost; the paper emphasizes their combination.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: Using Table 2, what two-part claim can you make about Transformer big on English-German?
lesson_steps.expected_response: Transformer big achieves 28.4 BLEU, higher than the listed previous models and ensembles. Its training cost is reported as 2.3 * 10^19 FLOPs, which is much lower than several prior ensemble costs while achieving better BLEU.
lesson_steps.remediation: Ask the learner to read one number from the BLEU column and one from the training-cost column. Then compare each against the previous systems in the same row group.

lesson_steps.title: Explain the empirical conclusion
lesson_steps.content: Assess whether the learner can state the conclusion without exaggerating beyond the table. A correct answer should be specific to the reported WMT 2014 tasks and the listed comparisons.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: What does Table 2 support about the Transformer on machine translation?
lesson_steps.expected_response: It supports that the Transformer achieves state-of-the-art or better BLEU on WMT 2014 English-German and English-French while requiring less training cost than many previous competitive models, especially compared with ensembles.
lesson_steps.remediation: Limit the claim to the tasks and models in Table 2. Then restate the two evidence columns: BLEU for quality and FLOPs for training cost.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: Table 2 is evidence for both quality and efficiency, not just a leaderboard. The big Transformer sets the strongest reported BLEU scores, while the base model already performs competitively at a much smaller training cost.

mastery_criteria: Reads BLEU and FLOPs from Table 2 to support a comparison.
Distinguishes base and big Transformer results.
States the empirical claim within the WMT 2014 evaluation scope.
common_difficulties: Treating BLEU improvements without considering training cost.
Overgeneralizing the table to all translation datasets or all model sizes.

units.title: What the model variations reveal
units.objective: Use Table 3 to infer how attention heads, dimensions, dropout, positional encoding, and model size affect Transformer performance.

lesson_steps.title: Why ablations matter
lesson_steps.content: After reporting strong results, the paper asks which architectural choices matter. Table 3 varies one or more settings from the base model and measures development perplexity, BLEU, and parameter count.

lesson_steps.title: How to read the table
lesson_steps.content: Unlisted values in each row match the base model, so each row group isolates a design change. The important comparisons are relative to the base row and to nearby variants in the same row group.

lesson_steps.title: Attention heads and key sizes
lesson_steps.content: Rows A vary the number of heads while keeping computation roughly constant; one head is worse than the base, but too many heads also reduces quality. Rows B show that reducing attention key size dk hurts model quality, suggesting compatibility computation is not trivial.

lesson_steps.title: Size, dropout, and positions
lesson_steps.content: Rows C and D support the authors' conclusion that bigger models are better and dropout helps avoid overfitting. Row E shows that learned positional embeddings perform nearly identically to sinusoidal encodings in this experiment.

lesson_steps.title: Interpret one ablation row group
lesson_steps.content: Have the learner turn a row group into a causal-style but cautious statement. The correct interpretation should say what changed and what metric changed, without claiming universal proof.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: What does row group E in Table 3 say about sinusoidal positional encoding versus learned positional embeddings?
lesson_steps.expected_response: Replacing sinusoids with learned positional embeddings gives nearly identical development results: PPL 4.92 and BLEU 25.7 versus base BLEU 25.8. The paper therefore chooses sinusoids mainly for possible extrapolation to longer sequences, not because Table 3 shows a large quality gap.
lesson_steps.remediation: Compare the base row and row E values directly. Then revisit Section 3.5's stated reason for choosing sinusoids despite similar results.

lesson_steps.title: Synthesize ablation conclusions
lesson_steps.content: Assess whether the learner can summarize multiple findings without flattening them into 'bigger is always better.' A strong answer includes the nuanced head-count result, key-size sensitivity, dropout usefulness, and positional-encoding comparison.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: List three conclusions supported by Table 3 about Transformer design choices.
lesson_steps.expected_response: Multiple heads help compared with one head, but too many can hurt; reducing dk hurts quality; larger models improve results; dropout is helpful; learned positional embeddings are nearly identical to sinusoidal encodings in the reported comparison.
lesson_steps.remediation: Prompt the learner to choose one conclusion from row groups A/B, one from C/D, and one from E. This structure prevents them from focusing on only model size.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: Table 3 shows that the Transformer's performance depends on several interacting design choices. It supports multi-head attention, sufficient key dimensions, dropout, and larger capacity, while showing that learned and sinusoidal positions performed similarly in this setting.

mastery_criteria: Reads Table 3 relative to the base row rather than as isolated numbers.
Explains the non-monotonic head-count result.
Summarizes at least three ablation-supported design conclusions.
common_difficulties: Assuming every increase in number of heads improves BLEU.
Mistaking nearly identical positional-encoding results for evidence that positions are unnecessary.

units.title: Generalization to English constituency parsing
units.objective: Explain how the paper uses constituency parsing results to support Transformer generalization beyond translation.

lesson_steps.title: Test beyond translation
lesson_steps.content: A model can excel on translation yet fail to generalize to other structured sequence tasks. The paper therefore evaluates the Transformer on English constituency parsing, where outputs are structurally constrained and longer than inputs.

lesson_steps.title: Parsing setup
lesson_steps.content: The authors train a 4-layer Transformer with dmodel = 1024 on the WSJ portion of the Penn Treebank. They also test a semi-supervised setting using larger high-confidence and BerkeleyParser corpora with about 17 million sentences.

lesson_steps.title: Read Table 4
lesson_steps.content: Table 4 reports WSJ Section 23 F1 scores. The Transformer reaches 91.3 in the WSJ-only discriminative setting and 92.7 in the semi-supervised setting, outperforming several previously reported systems in those categories.

lesson_steps.title: Not fully task-specialized
lesson_steps.content: The authors emphasize that they performed only a small number of tuning experiments for parsing. This matters because the result is presented as evidence of generality rather than as a heavily task-engineered parser.

lesson_steps.title: Connect setup to claim
lesson_steps.content: Ask the learner to explain why parsing is a meaningful transfer test. The answer should mention structural constraints and the fact that this is not simply another translation benchmark.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: Why does English constituency parsing provide evidence about Transformer generalization beyond translation?
lesson_steps.expected_response: It is a different sequence task with strong structural constraints and outputs longer than inputs. Good F1 results there suggest the architecture can work beyond machine translation.
lesson_steps.remediation: Point to Section 6.3's statement of parsing-specific challenges. Then ask how those challenges differ from translating one sentence into another sentence.

lesson_steps.title: State the supported conclusion
lesson_steps.content: Assess whether the learner can make a bounded generalization claim. They should cite the parsing evidence without claiming the paper proves success on every task.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: What conclusion about generalization is supported by the parsing experiments?
lesson_steps.expected_response: The experiments support that the Transformer can generalize to at least one non-translation structured sequence task, English constituency parsing, achieving competitive or better WSJ F1 results in WSJ-only and semi-supervised settings.
lesson_steps.remediation: Limit the conclusion to 'can generalize well to other tasks' as shown by this parsing task. Avoid universal claims and support the statement with the WSJ F1 results in Table 4.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: The parsing experiment extends the paper's evidence beyond WMT translation. A relatively lightly tuned Transformer performs strongly on WSJ constituency parsing, supporting the claim that attention-based sequence transduction is not translation-specific.

mastery_criteria: Describes the WSJ-only and semi-supervised parsing settings.
Uses Table 4 F1 results to support a generalization claim.
Avoids overclaiming beyond the paper's parsing evidence.
common_difficulties: Treating parsing as just another translation dataset.
Ignoring that the paper reports stronger systems still exist in some categories.

units.title: Interpreting learned attention heads
units.objective: Use the appendix visualizations to explain how attention heads may capture long-distance and structural sentence relations.

lesson_steps.title: Why visualize attention
lesson_steps.content: The paper notes interpretability as a side benefit of self-attention. The appendix visualizations show where different encoder self-attention heads place their attention in example sentences.

lesson_steps.title: What the figures show
lesson_steps.content: The visualizations connect tokens according to attention patterns from heads in encoder layer 5 of 6. Different colors or panels correspond to different heads, so the figures can illustrate specialization across heads.

lesson_steps.title: Long-distance dependency example
lesson_steps.content: Figure 3 focuses on attention from the word 'making.' Many heads attend to a distant dependency completing the phrase 'making ... more difficult,' illustrating how self-attention can connect far-apart positions directly.

lesson_steps.title: Anaphora-related example
lesson_steps.content: Figure 4 shows heads apparently involved in anaphora resolution around the word 'its.' The caption emphasizes that attentions for this word are sharp, meaning the distribution strongly focuses on particular tokens.

lesson_steps.title: Visualization is suggestive, not full proof
lesson_steps.content: The paper uses cautious language such as 'apparently involved' and 'seems related.' That means the visualizations support interpretability and qualitative insight, but they are not the same as a controlled causal proof of linguistic reasoning.

lesson_steps.title: Interpret a caption carefully
lesson_steps.content: Ask the learner to infer what a visualization supports without overstating it. The goal is to connect attention patterns to possible syntactic or semantic behavior while preserving the paper's caution.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: Figure 5 says many heads exhibit behavior that seems related to sentence structure. What is a careful interpretation of that claim?
lesson_steps.expected_response: Some heads learned distinct attention patterns that align with sentence-structure relations in the examples. This suggests interpretability and possible syntactic or semantic specialization, but the figure alone does not prove a complete grammar model.
lesson_steps.remediation: Highlight the words 'seems related' and 'examples.' Then ask the learner to state what the lines show directly before inferring what they may mean.

lesson_steps.title: Connect visualization to architecture
lesson_steps.content: Assess whether the learner can link the appendix back to multi-head self-attention. A correct answer should say that different heads can attend to different relations and that direct attention helps show long-distance dependencies.
lesson_steps.learner_prompt: How do the attention visualizations support the paper's claims about multi-head self-attention?
lesson_steps.expected_response: They show different heads attending to different tokens and relations, including long-distance dependencies and structure-related patterns. This supports the idea that multi-head self-attention can specialize across heads and provides some interpretability.
lesson_steps.remediation: Return to the multi-head claim that heads attend to different representation subspaces at different positions. Then point to Figures 3-5 as qualitative examples of different heads focusing on different relations.

lesson_steps.title: Durable takeaways
lesson_steps.content: The appendix visualizations qualitatively show that attention heads can focus on long-distance and structure-related relations. They strengthen the interpretability story for multi-head self-attention, but they should be read as illustrative evidence rather than exhaustive proof.

mastery_criteria: Interprets Figures 3-5 as examples of learned attention-head behavior.
Connects long-distance visual attention to self-attention's direct position-to-position paths.
States the interpretability claim cautiously, without overclaiming causal linguistic proof.
common_difficulties: Assuming every attention head has a human-interpretable linguistic role.
Treating qualitative attention plots as definitive proof of syntax or semantics.
